newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Andreatta rules out guarding Albanian vote.
newsitem.headline: Andreatta rules out guarding Albanian vote.

text.p: Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta on Saturday ruled out a direct role for the multinational force in guarding Albanian elections, but said it should provide security for international observers.
Andreatta told a news conference in the Albanian capital that all interested governments should begin analysing the role of the Italian-led force and decide in two weeks whether it needed changing.
The eight-nation, 6,000-strong force is securing deliveries of humanitarian aid in Albania, where anger over the collapse of pyramid savings schemes erupted in riots in February and March.

"It is clear that the armed multinational force does not have any direct task in the election process but should guarantee the security of the observers and by guaranteeing the security of the observers that will guarantee the security of the country in a particularly delicate day," Andreatta said.
The defence minister said the presence of the force had contributed to a restoration of normality in the Balkan state.

He welcomed the political contract hammered out between European envoy Franz Vranitzky and Albania's 10 main political parties on Friday, committing them to holding general elections by the end of June.
"Naturally, a touch of cynicism is necessary because Albanian politics is very complex," he said.
"But we hope that all the players understand that this is not a time for political games because the future of at least one generation of Albanians is at stake."
Andreatta told the Italian parliament last Wednesday that the multinational force should consider pulling out of Albania if the agreement to hold early general elections collapsed.

"If it is possible to stop the anarchy in a month or two, when it might be stoked if the elections are postponed, then the consequences for the political future of Albania would be very grave," he told the news conference.

Andreatta said the international community would be more ready to provide aid "if they have the sensation that Albanian political leaders can take up their responsibilities and know how to sacrifice the sweet games of politics in face of a national emergency."
He said thousands of international observers were needed for the elections "to reduce the amount of distrust".
"This is an action of the international organisations and so it is within the mandate of the force to protect them," he said.

The last general elections in Albania, in May 1996, were seen by international observers as seriously flawed. President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party won 122 seats in the 140 seat party and the opposition Socialists pulling out of the vote late on polling day.
But he emphasised that the mandate of the force did not allow it to operate as a police force.
"Are you aware what it would mean to Albanians if they heard stories of armed conflicts between foreigners and their citizens even if they were criminals, he said.
"What a chain of resentment and sense of frustration such a story would leave behind."
